headlines.title: Wildfire triggers evacuations in Sonoma County, shuts down stretch of Highway 1
headlines.description: A wildfire broke out along the coast of Sonoma County Thursday, prompting authorities to issue evacuation orders and shut down a portion of Highway 1. The wind-driven Woodside Fire burning near Salt Point State Park has scorched at least 100 acres in heavy timber, according to Cal Fire. Evacuation orders were issued for zone SON-1D1, Salt Point State Park, Steelwater Cove Regional Park, Ocean Cove Private Camp, and the Timber Cove Subdivision, according to Cal Fire. An evacuation warning was issued for zone SON-1D2. Highway 1 was shut down between Stewarts Point-Skaggs Springs Road and Timber Cove Road, officials said. This is a developing story. Details may change as more information becomes available. Stay tuned for updates. This story uses functionality that may not work in our app. Click here to open the story in your web browser.

headlines.title: Bay Area residents more likely to own homes after leaving region, study finds
headlines.description: Many Bay Area residents who leave the region are finding a more affordable path to homeownership, but often at the cost of lower incomes, lower-performing schools and greater climate risk, according to a new report released Thursday by a University of California research institute. The study by California Policy Lab found that people who move out of the Bay Area typically relocate to neighborhoods where home values are about 50% lower, and rents are about one-third cheaper than where they lived before. Residents who leave California are also 33% more likely to own a home five years after moving. Researchers said they analyzed anonymized consumer credit data to track Bay Area households over time, examining who leaves, where they move, and how their finances and neighborhoods change after relocating. Housing remains the Bay Area’s biggest financial challenge, according to the report. Nearly 40% of residents — including nearly half of renters — spend more than 30% of their income on housing. The median Bay Area home cost about $1.4 million in early 2026, compared with $915,000 statewide and $425,000 nationally. “The Bay Area continues to offer tremendous economic opportunity, but it’s also the most expensive metro in the country,” California Policy Lab executive director Evan White said in a statement. “Our research shows many residents are achieving affordable homeownership elsewhere, but often at the cost of lower incomes, lower-performing schools, or greater climate risk.” According to the report, Bay Area residents who move elsewhere in California or out of state generally end up in neighborhoods with lower average incomes and, for those remaining in California, schools with lower standardized test proficiency. Those leaving the region also tend to move to areas with that are more vulnerable to climate-related hazards such as wildfires, flooding and extreme heat. Researchers also found that residents leaving the Bay Area are not necessarily coming from its wealthiest or poorest neighborhoods. Instead, they generally leave neighborhoods that reflect the region overall but are, on average, in weaker financial shape than their neighbors, with credit scores 23 points lower and more than twice as much student debt. Migration is also changing the region’s demographics. White residents are leaving the Bay Area on net, while residents of color — particularly Asian and Pacific Islander households — are moving into the region in greater numbers or leaving at lower rates, making the Bay Area more racially diverse overall, researchers said. California Policy Lab researcher Brett Fischer said the findings raise broader questions about who can afford to live in the Bay Area as housing costs remain high and demand could increase further. “Our research strongly suggests that high housing prices are pushing people out, a trend that some fear may be exacerbated by the AI boom putting more pressure on housing prices,” Fischer said. Earlier this month, Gov. Gavin Newsom was in Oakland when he signed legislation aimed at lowering the cost of building affordable housing in California. The measure is expected to reduce construction costs by an estimated $60,000 to $70,000 per affordable housing unit by streamlining financing and reducing fees, while also extending state homelessness funding and creating a disaster rebuilding fund. Newsom lamented about how the state has historically not supported affordable housing. “We designed a system, a machine, over the course of the last half century to make it more difficult to build. It was intentionally designed, it wasn’t by chance, it wasn’t by happenstance. It was designed not to build. And that requires not just to think differently and argue for different results, but to rebuild the mission,” he said.

headlines.title: Power issue at BART's Pittsburg/Bay Point station causes delays
headlines.description: A PG&E power issue at BART’s Pittsburg/Bay Point station is causing delays for trains Thursday afternoon, according to the transit agency. BART initially reported the problem at about 1:45 p.m. and shortly after 2 p.m. said the power issue was causing delays of 20 minutes in both directions on the Antioch line. There is no estimate yet for when regular service will resume.

headlines.title: 1 injured after car crashes into San Jose business
headlines.description: Police are investigating after a vehicle crashed into a building in San Jose. The incident was reported at 11:39 p.m. in the 1700 block of Story Road, police said. Aerial coverage from NBC Bay Area’s SkyRanger showed half of a vehicle into the front of the Crawfish Bros business. Police said a person was taken to a hospital with non-life threatening injuries following the collision. The driver also remained on scene and is cooperating with the police investigation. No other information was immediately available. San Jose 23 hours ago San Jose 18 hours ago San Jose 24 hours ago Bicyclist injured following crash involving vehicle in San Jose

headlines.title: Randy's Donuts to open first Bay Area location – right next to a local favorite
headlines.description: Randy’s Donuts, a Los Angeles-based chain, is set to open its first Bay Area location in Santa Clara. Randy’s will open up shop at 2595 Homestead Rd. – right across the street from Stan’s Donut Shop, a local favorite since 1959. The grand opening of Randy’s is set for 7 a.m. Friday. The first 25 customers will get free doughnuts and swag from the owners. After that, all customers who arrive before 12 p.m. will receive a free glazed raised doughnut. Randy’s is known for its lengthy menu, which includes raised, buttermilk and premium doughnuts.

headlines.title: SFPD to step up patrols in Mid-Market following string of shootings
headlines.description: San Francisco is ramping up police patrols in the Mid-Market corridor following three shootings in a matter of days, leaders said Wednesday. The police department will increase its presence in the neighborhood through Monday, Aug. 3, as part of a high-visibility enforcement plan, San Francisco police Chief Derrick Lew said in a social media video posted by Supervisor Bilal Mahmood. The effort will include 24/7 officer foot patrols. “We know that visitors, residents, people that are doing business there don’t feel safe right now, so we’re addressing that,” Lew said. The three shootings, which do not appear to be connected, happened within a two-block stretch of Market Street, officials said. Police have made arrests in at least one of the shootings. “We had shooting incidents on Friday, then Saturday, then on Monday,” Lew said. “Truly concerning for us. A lot of good leads with those investigations. We’ve been working around the clock with our investigators and our officers, looking for suspects, further evidence, and things that we need to process for those investigations.” San Francisco Jul 28 San Francisco Jul 27 Police investigating shooting in San Francisco

headlines.title: Crash, downed power lines, brush fire snarl traffic in Novato
headlines.description: All lanes are open and electricity was restored to most PG&E customers in Novato on Thursday afternoon following an outage caused by a solo vehicle crash on U.S. Highway 101 earlier in the day. At about 9:20 a.m., an elderly woman was driving north in a white Jeep on Highway 101 when she hit a power pole near the state Route 37 interchange, according to California Highway Patrol spokesperson Officer Arthur Tellez. The woman suffered only minor injuries, but power lines came down across both sides of the highway and sparked small brush fires on the shoulders of both the northbound and southbound lanes, Tellez said. Traffic backed up for miles as PG&E crews worked to cut power to the lines so fire crews could get in and douse the flames. The collision and its aftermath left about 6,000 PG&E customers without power, according to utility spokesperson Megan McFarland, but by about 12:35 p.m., only about 700 customers were still affected. All lanes on Highway 101 were cleared by about 10:40 a.m. and all lanes to Route 37 were cleared by about 1 p.m.

headlines.title: SF Mayor Daniel Lurie signs largest city budget ever
headlines.description: San Francisco Mayor Daniel Lurie signed the city’s $16.9 billion budget Thursday, closing a $640 million budget deficit. Lurie signed the budget at a senior community center alongside several members of the San Francisco Board of Supervisors. The spending plan includes $34 million to help San Franciscans remain enrolled in Medi-Cal and CalFresh, $120 million for unhoused families, people living with HIV and AIDS, and LGBTQ+ community-based organizations, and $100 million set aside for potential state and federal cuts to housing and homelessness programs. It also provides $20 million to upgrade equipment for first responders and $71 million for projects including street resurfacing, drug treatment programs and mental health services. Lurie said the budget will help protect services as federal funding declines, while Supervisor Connie Chan said it reflects San Francisco’s values. City officials said the budget closes a two-year deficit and avoids a scenario in which the city’s deficit would have reached $1 billion within five years.

headlines.title: Foreign student visa restrictions to hit Silicon Valley
headlines.description: New federal regulations will restrict how long international students can attend U.S. colleges, and schools are scrambling to work through the problem as the fall semester begins. The U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has finalized a rule that limits most international students on F-1 visas and J-1 exchange visitor visas to a four-year education in the country, effective Sept. 15. San Jose State University will be hit hard, since most students need more than four years to complete their studies and the university counts on foreign student tuition to prop up its budget “We are currently working with the California State University system to assess the impact of the new rule for our international students,” a university spokesperson said in a statement. SJSU’s tuition for international undergraduates in the 2026-27 school year is $20,538 and $19,422 for graduate students, which is significantly higher than the cost for in-state undergrads at $9,553 and $10,944 for in-state post-grads. Last fall the school enrolled 2,538 foreign students and 2,332 this spring. The estimated annual tuition for those 4,870 students at the university would be close $49 million. A four-year visa limit will impede foreign students requiring additional time to complete their degrees, research, post-graduate studies or seeking employment in Silicon Valley following graduation. Current rules give students significantly more flexibility to complete academic programs, many of which are longer than four years. In a letter to foreign students, SJSU officials said the school’s International Student and Scholar Services is here to support them during this transition. Extensions will only be available through rigorous vetting, according to DHS. In a statement from DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin, he described the rule as cracking down on a loophole that international students were exploiting by extending their studies. “By implementing clear, finite limits on these visas, the United States is reclaiming its ability to properly screen, vet, and monitor individuals within our borders,” Mullin said. “This final rule ensures that foreign students remain focused on their primary purpose: completing their studies and returning home.” Many students at SJSU have to juggle work with school and can’t always get the classes they need to graduate in time. SJSU Junior Jeyan Lin, an accounting information system major, is concerned international students won’t be able to work in Silicon Valley following graduation. “For the school to have that diversity and feed into the industry is very important,” he told San Jose Spotlight. “Foreign students contribute culture and diversity. This is what is special about Silicon Valley, where the smartest people gather and create new technology.” Lin said high tech companies regularly recruit students from SJSU. He said if international students are deterred from attending, they’ll take their talents elsewhere — which would be a loss for San Jose and Silicon Valley. Sara, who asked to only use her first name for privacy reasons, is a marketing major going into her fifth year at San Jose State University. She said the new ruling will hurt the university and its students. “Being unsure about your status is extraordinarily stressful for these students,” she told San Jose Spotlight. “It’s important for colleges to stand up for our students and advocate for them.” During the last five years, the four-year graduation rate for all undergraduates was about 34% and about 78% for graduate students, the SJSU spokesperson said. San Jose State won’t be the only school in the region to be hit by the visa restrictions. At Santa Clara University, international students comprise 16% of graduate and professional students and 6% of undergraduates. In addition to the almost 1,000 enrolled international students, approximately 600 are employed through Optional Practical Training, a work program for F-1 visa holders. “Santa Clara University has a strong tradition of supporting the whole person and we extend this to our large and talented group of international students,” Susan Popko, vice provost for international programs at Santa Clara University, told San Jose Spotlight. William Sundstrom, an economics professor at Santa Clara University, said the university has many international graduate students in its business and law schools. Nationally, the median time of completion for bachelor’s degrees is more than four years for undergraduate students, he said, adding a large percentage of international students are enrolled in Ph.D. programs, which often take up to six years to complete. “A number of our grad students in business end up on Optional Practical Training visa extensions that are two years for STEM students and allows them to get a foothold in the Valley and then apply for an H-1B,” Sundstrom told San Jose Spotlight. “A lot of patents are issued to companies that have founders who are foreign-born. They’re integral to the tech ecosystem.” Sundstrom said the new visa restrictions negatively affect Silicon Valley’s economic prosperity and growth, as a large percentage of Silicon Valley entrepreneurs and nearly 70% of tech workers are foreign-born and many came to the U.S. as students. “We were already seeing some serious declines in international student enrollments,” he said. “The Trump administration’s general hostility to immigrants, both undocumented and documented, has created delays in the processes, denials of F-1 visa applications and a general sense of discouragement to come and study here.” Editor’s note: This story was originally published by San Jose Spotlight.

headlines.title: Father of boy rescued in Santa Cruz says he is beyond grateful to teen lifeguard
headlines.description: The father of a 10-year-old rescued from pounding surf off the Santa Cruz coast in a dramatic scene captured on video says he is beyond grateful to the teenage lifeguard who saved his son. “He ran into that water despite those conditions that are deadly. You have 10 foot waves; you have riptides and currents coming in,” Sumit Rai told The Associated Press on Wednesday. “It is not safe for him to go into that water. So he’s risking his own safety.” Rai’s son Nathaniel was standing in shallow water when he lost his footing and was pulled into the ocean Saturday by powerful swells that suddenly came ashore at Seabright Beach in Santa Cruz, about 60 miles down the coast from San Francisco. Rai, who was in his home city of Dallas, said he heard about what happened when he spoke to his kids on the phone that evening. “My son told me that he drowned and my son told me that he went unconscious,” he said. “He was very subdued, still in a state of shock.” By the next morning, Rai had watched the video of the rescue that has since caught the attention of President Donald Trump. Ryder Williams, 16, the lifeguard who saved Nathaniel, said he saw the boy lose his footing in ankle-deep water. He radioed in and then raced toward Nathaniel. “After the first wave, I was unable to pull him out because he was limp and the waves were pushing so hard,” he said in a statement. California State Parks, which employs the lifeguards at that beach, said the boy was swept about 15 yards into the ocean before the lifeguard made contact with him. Santa Cruz 20 hours ago Santa Cruz Jul 28 Santa Cruz Jul 27 In the video, Williams can be seen diving into a coming wave while holding tight to the boy. Another lifeguard jumped in to help, along with some bystanders, who Williams said he warned to go back to the shore. “I’m grateful to have had the opportunity to return the child to his family safely,” he said. “This is my job and I love what I do. I’m thankful to my fellow lifeguards who perform rescues just like this every day.” The boy had no serious injuries, and after an medical evaluation he was released to his family, the California State Parks said in an emailed statement. Rai said his son told him that he got sand in his lungs and was coughing it out after getting to the shore. Now his son, who is expected back from California in a few days, is dealing with the psychological effects of what happened. “He’s still been thinking about it a lot. It’s on his mind,” he said. “It bothers him when he’s sleeping. So it’s obviously traumatizing.” Rai has reached out to Williams and said he hopes to be able to thank him directly. “What he did, I can never ever repay,” he said. “I’m forever grateful.”

headlines.title: San Francisco city attorney takes aim at hotel booking scams
headlines.description: San Francisco City Attorney David Chiu filed a lawsuit Wednesday against two hotel booking sites that have been allegedly scamming travelers into paying substantially higher prices for hotel rooms. The defendants in the case are GuestReservations.com and BookOnline.com. In the suit, the city attorney’s office is alleging that these sites advertise online as if they are authentic hotel booking sites, but instead are trying to rip off tourists and trick them into paying more for hotel rooms. The city is also suing Booking Holdings, the websites’ hotel room inventory supplier that allegedly assisted in the scam. BookOnline.com, GuestReservations.com, and Booking Holdings could not be reached for a comment. When using GuestReservations.com and BookOnline.com, travelers end up paying 35 to 85% more in markups, according to the city attorney’s office. GuestReservations.com and BookOnline.com have received thousands of complaints across review websites. “It’s time to stop the scam and help Californians get their money back,” said Chiu during a press conference at City Hall. According to Chiu, when people end up using these sites and pay inflated rates for hotels, it hurts local businesses as tourists have less money to spend during their trips to the city. “We’re asking a court to end these unlawful business practices, to secure restitution for Californians who are overcharged, and to impose civil penalties to ensure that companies don’t repeat misconduct,” Chiu added. The city attorney’s office is asking anyone who is a victim of these scams or has more information to reach out to the office’s consumer complaint portal online at https://digital.forms.sf.gov/complaint, or call 415-554-3977.
headlines.source: Lloyd B. Davis | Bay City News

headlines.title: At 60, Too $hort has no plans to stop his hip-hop voyage with new album produced fully by Lil Jon
headlines.description: At 60, Too $hort is helping usher hip-hop into what he calls its senior citizen era. Just don’t expect him to rap like one. The Oakland hip-hop pioneer is still recording, touring and talking slick more than four decades after he began selling homemade tapes on the streets of the Bay Area. While the genre has long treated aging like an unwritten career-ending offense, Too $hort is breaking the rule and challenging the culture’s elder statesmen to keep going with him. His latest proof is “Sir Too $hort Vol. 2: Drink & Smoke,” his 23rd studio album, produced entirely by longtime collaborator Lil Jon. It arrives Friday, exactly 20 years after the release of his enduring hit “Blow the Whistle.” Too $hort, whose catalog also includes classics like “The Ghetto” and “Shake That Monkey,” says he isn’t interested in slowing down anytime soon. That was certainly evident when he and E-40 performed at the NFL Honors in February. In an interview with The Associated Press this week, Too $hort reflected on turning 60, challenging hip-hop’s age limits, preserving the legacy of Lil Jon’s late son, DJ Young Slade, the staying power of “Blow the Whistle” and why he has no plans to stop until “the wheels fall off.” This interview has been edited for length and clarity. AP: You recently turned 60, but you’re still releasing albums, touring and influencing the culture. When you first started selling homemade tapes on the streets of Oakland, did you ever imagine you’d still be doing this more than four decades later? TOO $HORT: At the age of 14 or 15, my mentality was, “Let people hear this music. We’re going to rock some house parties and high school dances and sell some tapes to fans in the streets.” When I got my foot in the door, I knew this was going to be my job. It was always “till the wheels fall off.” It was never, “Let’s do this for 30 or 40 years.” I’ve always said the day hip-hop is no longer my job is probably the day I’ll stop. But the love I have for hip-hop won’t allow me to stop recording. I’ve never taken a long break. I’ve continuously been in the studio, continuously doing shows. I just keep it going because it’s my job. AP: Why do you think you’ve remained relevant when so many careers have come and gone? TOO $HORT: I truly love making music. It’s never felt like work. I could have stopped after “Blow the Whistle” and been like, “Story told.” But somebody’s got to go out into these uncharted waters and blaze the trail. Look at E-40,Snoop Dogg,Fat Joe and the other guys who kept going after the kids were grown and the grandkids were on the way. Who laid the rule down that in hip-hop you gotta stop at 40? Every milestone they said was old. First it was 30, then it was 40, then it was 50. Now we got senior citizen rappers, and this … is real. Hip-hop is entering the place where jazz, blues and R&B have older artists who are still performing and recording. We should too. AP: Twenty years after its release, “Blow the Whistle” is still played everywhere from NBA arenas to the Olympics. Why do you think that record has endured? TOO $HORT: I don’t know if you could give me the ingredients and tell me how to do it again; I don’t think I could. It had to happen organically. I give Lil Jon a lot of credit because he’s made a lot of songs we’ve loved since the day they came out. We make good music together, and that’s why I’m excited for people to hear what we’re still doing 30 years after we first worked together. AP: This album reunites you with Lil Jon, but it also features work from his late son, Slade, who died in February. What did that collaboration mean to you? TOO $HORT: His son passed away after we finished recording. We had actually done about twice as many songs as ended up on this project. I saw how it affected Jon, and I had recently lost my brother, so I knew that feeling of loss. The whole time, Slade was producing or co-producing a lot of the tracks I was working on. The first thing that came to me was that I’d be more than proud to be part of his son’s legacy and give something to the world that would help him live forever. Jon keeps saying, “Slade’s legacy,” and I’m just trying to be a part of that and show the world we lost another good, talented person. AP: You and E-40 celebrated Bay Area hip-hop together during your 2020 Verzuz appearance. Fans still love seeing you two together. Would you ever team up again, whether for another Verzuz, a tour or something else? TOO $HORT: We did one in 2020, but it wasn’t a battle. We had a good time. We did a lot of laughing, a lot of togetherness. I didn’t want to battle 40 then, and I don’t want to battle him now. That’s my best friend in hip-hop. I’d sign up for me and 40 against anybody. That’d be fun. They haven’t had two groups. … I put that out there: Who wants to battle Too $hort and E-40 in Verzuz?
headlines.source: Jonathan Landrum Jr. | The Associated Press
